answer_text:
## AltaVista — The Rise and Fall of a Search Pioneer

**AltaVista** (meaning *"high view"* in Spanish) was once one of the most important search engines on the internet. Here's its full story:

---

### 🚀 Origins (1995)
AltaVista was created by researchers at Digital Equipment Corporation (DEC) who were trying to showcase the company's hardware and make it easier to find files on the company's public network. Launched in December 1995, it was the first "full text" / boolean searchable index of the World Wide Web.

At launch, AltaVista had two key innovations: a fast, multi-threaded web crawler called **Scooter** that could cover far more web pages than were believed to exist, and an efficient backend database called **TurboVista** running on advanced hardware.

---

### 📈 Peak Popularity
Web traffic increased steadily from 300,000 hits on the first day to more than 80 million hits per day by 1997, making it one of the most popular websites at the time.

As late as 2000, AltaVista was still more popular than Google, holding 17.7% of the search market compared to Google's 7%.

In 1996, AltaVista became the exclusive provider of search results for Yahoo. In 1997, it launched **Babel Fish**, a web-based machine translation application that translated text or webpages.

---

### 📉 The Decline
In 1998, Digital was sold to Compaq, and in 1999, Compaq redesigned AltaVista as a web portal in a last-ditch effort to compete with Yahoo. Under CEO Rod Schrock, it abandoned its streamlined search page and transformed itself into a web portal, diluting its core search function with features like shopping and email.

This backfired drastically. By focusing on becoming a full-fledged web portal, AltaVista diluted its core strength: search.

In December 1999, AltaVista filed for a $300 million initial public offering; it was cancelled due to the end of the dot-com bubble.

---

### 🔄 Multiple Ownership Changes
In June 1999, Compaq sold 83% of AltaVista to CMGI for $2.1 billion in stock and $220 million in cash.

In February 2003, Overture Services acquired AltaVista for $140 million. In July 2003, Yahoo acquired Overture for $1.63 billion.

From that point on, AltaVista became a zombie brand — a shell that used Yahoo!'s search technology but maintained its old look. No innovation, no updates, no real purpose.

---

### 💀 The End (2013)
The official closure happened quietly on **July 8, 2013**. No farewell. No headlines. Just a redirect to Yahoo.com.

---

### 🏆 Legacy
AltaVista wasn't killed by bad technology — it was killed by bad strategy. Had it stuck to what it did best — search — it might have had a fighting chance.

AltaVista is also credited with implementing the **first CAPTCHA** to prevent fraudulent account registrations and bots from automatically adding pages to its web index.

AltaVista was truly the Google of its era — a revolutionary tool that helped define how the world navigated the early internet.
